name: Griffin
dek: Touch without meaning.
pages: I met Griffin at a cuddle convention. The premise, supposedly, is that cuddling can be platonic -- "touch without meaning." Reader, I am here to report that a cuddle convention, put on by a lot of shitty people as a sad excuse for not having a valentine on Valentine's Day, is not the place where this is likely to take place. Alpha and I had just met and "moved in" together, and we'd decided we weren't staying home; hypothetically, we both wanted to find love. On the bus we made fun of a woman who got on and off with us, then realized she was going exactly where we were going. Then, outside political-correctness headquarters, Alpha joked to a stranger that the whole consent conversation was bullshit that didn't need half an hour -- and we walked in, and she was standing at the front of the room, speaking. Behind her, a chalkboard of polite ways to say no. First we practiced rescinding consent. She tried to make it fun by inventing cuddle positions -- the alligator, where one person's legs open like an alligator's mouth -- but the fun was mostly ruined by Alpha sweating nervously at the back. Then, the second layer of hell: the actual cuddle room, where you discuss, with the people you're about to cuddle, what saying no feels like. Lucky me, my partner was one of the organizers. I asked if I could touch her hair. She said, "no, because I don't think you would be comfortable with that" -- then raised her hand and announced to the whole group that she'd said no because she didn't really think I wanted to touch her hair. Pointing at me. The creepy one, who'd asked for what they could not have.

Then we pretended to be animals -- crawling like hippos, cuddling like giraffes. Most people were cats or dogs, which I supposed was the point: the platonic cuddle made flesh. I was a sloth. I did not move at all. I waited for the torture to be over. In the final round I inadvertently found the one attractive male in this sea of potential cuddlers, and perhaps he'd done the same, because we gravitated slowly toward each other -- a tall boy with a blonde ponytail -- along with a woman who told us she was asexual but still liked human contact. Pillow talk was hopping in our little cuddle threesome, what with him trying to hit on me without hitting on her: we discussed how much we enjoyed that one could cuddle platonically, nothing sexual about it at all, as his hand snaked slowly toward my butt and I moved it gently away. Then came the Valentine's dance, preceded by a barbaric form of slam poetry where the audience stands on their chairs to vote for the poem they liked best -- a great idea, unless your poem did badly and you stared out at a crowd of the seated. I never did like slam poetry, so I stayed in my seat. In the spirit of the convention we held hands the whole way to the dance -- myself, the tall blonde boy, a girl with straight hair, and Alpha. A little hard to pass a four-person cuddle monster on the sidewalk, but, as I always say, "cuddling trumps passerby traffic." At the dance, Griffin ignored me and flirted with the girl to his left -- a petite brunette in glasses and a bright red dress. All evening you could watch his mind turning, working the problem of getting the two of us into bed with him together. I wasn't necessarily opposed -- not because I was interested in her, but it seemed like an interesting experience to navigate, figuring out what my role would be. She was less interested, and left him for a boy who turned up near the end in a motorcycle helmet, who was, ostensibly, already her partner.

Upstairs, over a cider he'd bought, Griffin made a speech about how much power he had, his ability to control people, and how interested I was in having sex with him -- then asked me how much I wanted to. I had been thinking no such thing, and told him so, and he backtracked, embarrassed. He also liked the barbarian lifestyle: in some situations he might act barbaric, or barbarous, if the situation fit -- circumstantially only, he insisted; normally he was civilized. Then he laid out his plan to bed me and the other girl together, and, for the sake of being unpredictable, I agreed -- but first I wandered off to take a call from my brother, who reported he'd seen two salamanders making love in an aquarium that day. God's Valentine's Day gift to the world. Talking to my brother, my voice changed into the voice of someone familiar, someone with things in common, and I think it put my date off. Downstairs, Griffin asked her whether she wanted to do this. She said no. Then we both danced with other people. Whatever energy there had been had clearly dissipated, but the plan was the plan, so we left together and got on a bus toward his house. At his street I told him I wanted to go home, and he asked if it was because I was afraid he'd force me to do something I wasn't comfortable with. I said that was the case. He assured me he would do no such thing, so I agreed, apprehensively. At his house we cuddled on the couch, discussing once more the advantages of cuddling outside a romantic or sexual context. He carried me to his room; I insisted I no longer wanted to have sex with him. We got naked and did not do anything sexual. In the morning I looked at his extensive Lego collection and he made me eggs, then played a video game while I talked to my friend Alessio. A few months later I ran into him at a party, but I was with another boy, and I didn't want to talk to him.

name: David
dek: A cat between us.
pages: David's photos were abnormal, emphasizing his creamy complexion. He seemed very young for a man -- he was in fact two years younger than me -- but we'd bantered about cats and dreams, so I agreed to meet him at an all-night coffee house I rarely visited during the day. When I arrived he'd already ordered, and stood as far from the counter as humanly possible, so as not to be confused for the one paying. I ordered a chai. We sat at a round table and he talked about studying computer science, and I remember thinking, for some reason, that this could be the one. Then I got annoyed, because he wasn't making conversation -- I was talking fast, asking questions, and he was sitting far back in his chair, quiet. I said I shouldn't finish my chai or I'd get even more hyper. He said I should drink the rest and see how hyper I could get, which didn't match the impression I'd been getting, so I gave him a few points, and let him finish it instead. At the bus stop I hugged the pole of the bus sign and swung around it and said this was the same as paying the fare, while he stood upright, checking his phone, nervous the bus wouldn't come on time. He refused to tell me his height in anything but centimeters -- something about the system being flawed -- and took this strange hill much further than I would have guessed. Reader, I still don't know how tall he is.

At his house he told me his roommate had never once brought a date over, so all this was very surprising to him. They had beef: both vegetarian, but she'd gone vegan and was now shaming him for keeping butter in the fridge. I couldn't imagine how two such polite people had come to harbor such total and complete resentment. Then we made pasta, and he handed me a giant block of cheddar to grate, and when I switched to a second, larger grater that worked better, he became very pissy that I'd used two cheese graters. Two graters to clean, instead of one. I was starting to see how he might be having difficulty getting along with his roommate. She came home peppy, with her date; they cuddled on the couch with beers and put on Lost in Translation. Beside the couch was a seat salvaged from a car, lever and all. David sat in the car chair, said nothing further, refused the beer -- I accepted mine -- and when they floated a second movie he said that they could, but that he didn't want to, and that he could take me home if I wanted. In the garage he had a motorcycle. It was at that moment I realized I had to pee, which wouldn't do for my first time on a motorcycle. He'd forgotten our helmets inside, so, panicked, I squatted in his shed hoping to finish before he came back, but the thought of him reappearing made me pee-shy. He came out, handed me a helmet, and we rode home, and it was exhilarating. Then we decided to play chess outside; the backyard sheds wouldn't open, and eventually we abandoned the game and stood awkwardly in the kitchen, saying goodbye without touching. The next time he picked me up, we drank beer at the park, went back to his and played Nooki and fell asleep holding hands, a cat between us. I dreamt there was another girl in our bed -- Molly, maybe -- who looked like his cat.

name: Jake
dek: A hot babe on my lap.
pages: Through the window of the Southeast Grind, at ten o'clock at night, I saw the most attractive person I had ever encountered, outside, having a cigarette. I figured he was passing through. I figured I would never talk to him or anything. Instead he came and sat three seats away at the counter, drawing in a sketchbook, and one by one the people between us left, until it was just him and me. So I sprawled crazily across all three empty seats, stomach on the middle one, and asked if I could see what he was drawing. He showed me. It wasn't anything particularly impressive -- a washed-out nature scene, in watercolor -- and immediately I was turned off. But I was already there, sprawled across three seats. He asked if I wanted to play chess. Of course. He got the board from the games closet and set it up in an interested silence -- he never asked whether I knew how to play, or whether I was any good, which flattered me. A few moves in I got bored, and started to act out. Rather than moving my pawn two spaces, I moved it three. He said nothing. He took his turn. I took mine. I moved a knight into a cluster of his pieces. I moved his pieces. I moved two of my own at once. I returned dead pieces to the board. Finally I killed my king with my own queen and moved it off the board, so that no one could win -- and we continued anyway, until he had about ten pieces left and I had one white pawn darting around all of them, whether it was my turn or not. "You win," I said. He agreed, and set up the board again. I won the second game. Through all of it he stayed stony-faced and unperturbed, following the rules without comment.

Outside, I leaned on him, his dark sweatshirt against mine, the cigarette in his hand. He sat down and had me sit on his lap. A friend came over and asked how he was. "Can't complain," Jake said. "I got a hot babe on my lap and a hot cigarette on my lips." He pulled at the lining of my dress -- "Is this a... scarf?" -- and leaned in to kiss my mouth, but I turned my head the other way, so that we would not be intimate. Then I turned around and put my arms around his neck and my legs around his stomach. "You're a little koala, aren't you?" he said, in something like disbelief. He was an artist, he said; the Grind was the only place open all night, and he liked to work on his art there. Then we were walking to his studio downtown, a long walk, into streets I'd seldom explored, him carrying my Thomas the Tank Engine backpack in his hand like a clutch. "Is there anything you want to know about me?" he asked, finally, into the silence. We passed a garbage-disposal building. "I used to work there," he said. At the studio he made noodles in a silver cylinder with a pouring spout, in what I could not imagine were clean pans, and handed me the aux cord. I put on Gucci Mane. "You like Gucci Mane?" he asked, surprised. He offered me noodles; I shook my head no; and just as he was almost done eating, I said, "actually, can I have some?" As soon as he'd finished, he said, "Hey -- do you wanna go to my loft?" I didn't answer. He was already climbing the ladder. It was dark up there, and we looked at each other, and it just happened that we started kissing, and he stopped to replace the wooden board that was the door to the ladder. "You're the first girl I've brought here," he said, with a goofy grin.

In the morning he said he had to get up in a little bit, and I sat up and started collecting my phone and clothes, and he put his hand around my waist and pulled me backwards, so that I was curled up in front of him. "We can sleep a bit more." The room was warm and soaked in sun, and I enjoyed being held in place. When we finally got up, a whiff of insanity came over me, an extreme airiness; I felt better watching him lace his combat boots back onto his feet, pulling each lace tight. I imagined they were steel-toed. He asked if I wanted to take a shower and I said "yeah!" -- and then, when I tried to come into the shower with him, he explained, as though I were a child, that some experiences were personal, and that he liked to shower by himself. Afterwards, through the bathroom door, I listened to Jake and a voice I didn't recognize invent, together, a wooden butt plug. I'll spare you their reasoning. He walked me to the nearest street corner. "So, did you want my number?" I went through the motions of putting him in my phone, first name only, since I didn't know his last and didn't care to ask. He seemed to notice, and told me he rarely gives girls his number. I hugged him around the middle and said "bye," and walked, rather purposefully, away -- into a part of downtown Portland I'd never been to. I called Adam, who was high and bored and not interested in my experience. I called Charlie, who was mean to me for reasons I couldn't locate. I sat alone at a four-person table in a greasy Chinese place, eating a few bites of fried beige noodles -- too salty, the noodles too fried. Then a text came from Alessio: our somewhat romantic friendship made him feel he was cheating on his girlfriend, and he could no longer be friends with me. My stomach dropped. I started walking slowly toward home, and somewhere along the side of the highway I stopped being upset and was just sad, which is different. I found a bus stop I knew, and it was so easy to get home -- all I had to do was wait for the bus to get there. I spent a quiet night at home.

name: Blake
dek: Points for pretending I didn't speak Spanish.
pages:
Blake set the date in the middle of a forest. He gave me intentionally obscure directions to meet him on a fallen tree at a trail in downtown Portland, and this, I supposed, was exactly the quirky premise I'd been hoping for, which is, of course, why I agreed. I didn't let myself set an alarm, even though I was to meet him at ten. Google Maps wasn't working on my phone, so I had my roommate plan my route on his computer, and then I got on the bus and rode it to the completely wrong end of town.
In my defense, the sun was slanting through the windows and I got wrapped up in wondering what all the other passengers might be doing on this strange day. People with lives, I supposed. I didn't have one. It reminded me of days I'd been excused from school with a doctor's note and allowed to lounge on the sunny couches in my parents' bedroom, the sun hitting them from an unfamiliar angle, reality shifted a fraction of an inch into an alternate reality where things, vaguely, weren't as they often were. I stared at the spot on the map that was supposed to be my hiking trail, saw only concrete, and decided I must be crazy to imagine that beyond all these streets I'd find myself in an all-consuming wilderness. So I stayed seated.
When I realized my mistake, I panicked. Waves of caution I hadn't felt since I nervously awaited a teacher's realization that I had not, as instructed, written six pages. It was a wake-up call. Why were there exactly zero moments of this kind of terror in my daily life? I couldn't remember the last time I'd felt this alive, and though it wasn't pleasant, I resolved to do more things. The vaguest of plans. I texted him that I was lost. He said he was enjoying what he was doing in his tree, and that it would still be there when I got there. A lot of points for him.
The rest of the directions said: past three fallen trees, across two wooden bridges, and I'd find him. I hadn't come to even one of the markers. I went back. I texted him. I went forward. I sat down on the trail and, though my battery was low, listened to Blue by Animal Collective, to collect myself. Two women confirmed there were, in fact, wooden bridges a little farther up. I walked the way I'd been going all along, got confused again, and called him.

He agreed to meet me at the entrance, where I gulped from the water fountain with complete delight, like a deer at a watering hole, which is something I feel like almost all the time anyway. I had made him wait on his tree for two hours. He arrived in a punk-rock t-shirt, hair long, healthy height and weight, not particularly set on impressing me. Neither of us acknowledged the strangeness of the meeting place. We kept going.
We went to get a burger. On the way he told me all about his weed-trimming business, how good it was for him, how he didn't feel guilty about it, and I said nothing, because I was not remotely interested. He also gave me a long description of the difference between mda and mdma. I didn't let him pay. I already knew I didn't like him, and it wouldn't have been fair to accept free food without reciprocating.
We played a game where we each wrote parts of stories on the little pads of paper from my purse, and I lied about not speaking Spanish to prove a point I was making. He asked, on a scale of one to ten, how the date was going for me. I declined to answer. About a seven for him, he said. I'd earned points for persevering on the hike, and for pretending I didn't speak Spanish to make a racist point. Then he told me he'd written his ex-girlfriend's senior thesis for her, because she was Asian and couldn't write English that well.
There was a couch, and a mirror, and his arm around me, and we might have kissed. I said I was really tired and just wanted a nap. This was true. At my house I lay down on my bed. He came in and seemed uncomfortable, said this wasn't what he'd been expecting, said he wanted to cuddle. I said I really just wanted to nap, because I was by then a little disgusted by him, by how much he had talked. But his trying to convince me made me reconsider, because it was an interesting thing, arguing that we should cuddle, until finally he asked if he was ever going to see me again. I said no. He said alright, fine.
I walked him to the bus stop and waved goodbye when he got on. That night I went to the Southeast Grind, and Jake was there, flirting with a blonde girl on the couch. They left together. He ignored me.

name: Louis
dek: Caturday.
pages: Louis was so very cute in all of his pictures, and I couldn't believe he'd want to meet me. He said something about it being "Caturday" -- the day for cats. In person he was cute too, and very lovely, and immediately claimed my roommate's giant yoga ball, bouncing, while I took the rolly chair. He'd started doing yoga recently. He liked dancing. We went to Buffalo Exchange on Hawthorne, where he tried on leggings -- though first we tried on hats together -- and then, while he waited in the chair beside me, I applied for a job, filling out the application until someone came over and interviewed me on the spot. We had trouble finding the car and it was starting to rain. We found a Mexican restaurant with almost a tiki theme, extravagant vegetation climbing to the ceiling, and I was confused about which cocktail to order, not being used to ordering cocktails, so we each chose something different and shared. He told me about his old relationship -- five years, ended by small things going wrong -- and then said he felt bad for talking so long. No, I said. It was interesting. Keep going. So he told me about his next adventure, in which he would go pick weed leaves and then take ayahuasca. He drove me home to change my pants and then took me to a dance club I'd never been to called Bossa Nova: a live band of three probably elderly gentlemen, disco lights in the floor, booths where people drank extravagant cocktails and maybe even smoked cigars. We ended up smack in the middle of the dance floor, where it was very hot, and though we were dancing together, he had yet to so much as grab my wrist. This went on for a long while as I contemplated what might be going on -- this seemed an obvious time to invite physical contact -- until I said fuck it, broke the rules, and leaned my hand casually on his hip. Then we got two more drinks each and started making out in a booth. He drove us back through the rain, and we made out in the car, and his fingers traveled southward, and he asked if I wanted to go inside. Inside, we almost went further, but he asked if I wanted to, and I said no, so we didn't. He rolled over and slept completely separate from me, falling asleep quickly while I watched his slow breathing. He left fairly early the next morning.

name: Patrick
dek: Like a tiger, or a man proving a point.
pages: I meet Patrick on the street; he has just come from the 7-Eleven with a beer. Carefully constructed hipster: lumberjack plaid flannel, large horn-rimmed frames, and a messy bun perched on his silky mane of light ginger strands. I'm wearing my customary black tight dress, black skeleton long-sleeve, black Harley-Davidson boots -- all of it, for the past week and a half, because none of my other clothes are clean. On our way we pass Michael at a table in front of an open laptop, wearing his signature gray cardigan and what seems to be his only t-shirt, the tiny holes making it possible to see part of his bare chest shining translucent in the moonlight. He joins us for more beer. I buy a very dark porter in a handsome glass bottle -- not a single beer but a 40, much too much for me to drink by myself, but I'm feeling ambitious. Outside, I find the two of them amiably comparing notes on what they hate about America, gesturing rapidly, the word capitalism interjected every few seconds. Both want to move as soon as possible, maybe to China or India, where things are cheaper and more community-oriented and there isn't so much capitalism. I can't quite bring myself to join. I stare instead at the bumps in the paved lot, and at the white poles holding up the canopy, and at the dark night behind it all. The more the merrier, you might think. But no: my friend and my date claim each other's attention entirely, leaving none for yours truly. Then a stranger pulls up in a beat-up van and, while his car fills with gas, approaches me -- only me -- to ask if I have a cigarette. Gauges, a nose piercing, khaki shorts. I am, frankly, pleased to finally have a companion of my own. Patrick says he'll give him one for fifty cents. The stranger digs fifty cents from his pocket. Cigarette acquired, he goes back to ignoring my two companions, looks straight at me, and asks, quite aggressively, who these boys are. I answer frankly: I'm on a date with one; the other is my friend. He glances at Patrick just long enough to gesture at him, and asks whether I feel safe with my date.

"Look, you can't just, like, insult my date like that or whatever, ok. He's, like, a person and all." I am hoping this confrontation might at least have the effect that no one utters the word capitalism for the rest of the night. Michael says nothing and does nothing, a shit-eating grin plastered across his face. Patrick stalks closer and closer to the stranger, until he is centimeters from his head, staring with his magnificent dark eyes. Like a tiger. Or like a man trying to prove a point. "If we were to fight -- just saying -- you'd be dead. On the ground in one second." Then he wraps his arm lightly around the stranger's back: "You guys look gay. Oh look, I think they're gay -- don't you think they might be, like, maybe just a little bit gay, or something? No? I think they might be." Michael and I stare at each other across the circle, a hint of mirth on our lips and confusion in our eyes, as our two new friends square up to fight each other over nothing. Finally I say to the stranger, "do you, like, really wanna hit something, or what? Cause, you can just hit me." He doesn't believe me at first. "It'll be fine, I think. No, seriously." We go back and forth until he delivers a light slap to the side of my face -- not so light as I was expecting. After that, I can think of nothing to do but leave, and so Patrick and I make our way home, while the stranger presumably returns to his van and Michael, from the corner of my eye, seats himself at a nearby picnic table. Tension successfully diffused. To what end, exactly, I can't be sure. At home, I fulfill my promise of letting him sleep in my bed -- except he isn't ready to sleep. I simply want to. Patrick lies awake beside me, pleading that I haven't gotten a chance to know him, that I've prejudged him, that I've made a mistake. In the morning he smokes out of a pipe he brought and leaves the ashes on our communal table, where my roommate -- this is a substance-free household -- sees them before I can. He texts me later, thanking me for the show. I can only suppose how his account might differ from mine. Still, I think he would be the main character, since I can't think of anything out of the ordinary that I said or did.

name: Trevor
dek: He smashed a beer bottle over his own head.
pages: Trevor called before the date with a question: did I have any ex-boyfriends who might be out to get him? Someone had just phoned and threatened him not to go out with his girl. I told him I wasn't sure who it could be, but assumed it wasn't related to me. He didn't sound convinced. He sounded a little angry -- at me, somehow, already. He showed up twenty minutes later anyway and ordered a coffee with four shots. Very cute, not very big, a bit like Drake from Drake and Josh, skinny jeans and a black t-shirt. We drove to The Florida Room and took the outdoor patio, where he bought us tequila shots and we read our poetry to each other. He knew the bartender -- the bartender who always poured him extra-full shots -- which is how I came to be very drunk, drifting over to other people's tables to talk with them for a while and then inform them they were boring, until Trevor escorted me out. His house was two blocks away; he lived on the top level, and I made a lot of noise in the bathroom. On the stairs up to his attic room, the light caught something on his face: scratches. I asked about them -- though I only know that because he told me the next day; by then the night had gaps in it. His ex-girlfriend had done something to upset him, he said, so he'd smashed a beer bottle over his own head, to try to kill himself. A strange story to tell on a first date. He offered it easily, like it was nothing. In the morning he handed me the remote and said I could put on any movie I wanted, so I put on Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. The sun came in sweet and yellow, and the colors were so pastel and opaque that I decided it was my favorite movie; as it went on, I liked it less, and realized there was sort of no plot. On his ceiling was an electrical outlet, and when he plugged his phone into it, the phone dangled there in the air, pretty far down, turning slowly on its cord. I watched it instead of the movie.

He had a therapy appointment that afternoon -- he'd have to drop me off after breakfast. We ate big breakfasts, and in traffic on the bridge he called his therapist to say he'd be running late; his therapist, he told me, really liked him, and wouldn't mind. By the time we arrived the appointment had already passed, so he called back and -- since it was all the way across town -- apologized, and cancelled. We went back to his place and watched television instead. He told me about Mount St. Helens -- how a man had caught the eruption in a photograph and sold it to the newspapers for a fortune -- and I was amazed, so we went to the computer and he showed me the pictures. He told me the story of his ex-girlfriend as we walked. They'd been homeless together for a while, and it had made them very close; now that he had a place to live, she treated him like shit -- never letting him talk to other girls, breaking up with him to go out with other boys, then calling to say mean things. He'd been meaning to break up with her, he said. They kept getting back together. We set out for a strip club across the bridge, but he got too tired, so we turned around. The walk back was quiet, and he played Venus in Furs on his iPhone -- that thin little speaker our only company -- and we both knew the words, so we sang along. Later a friend texted him about a night club. The floor was white with lights underneath it, like that game with the polar bears -- don't break the ice -- and girls danced on poles, climbing down every once in a while to mingle with the crowd. A guy came up to chat me up -- Palestinian, I think -- and kept telling me I was too cute to bomb. I declined his offer of a drink. Trevor and I sat out on the curb while he smoked, watching a couple change clothes, or have sex, in a jeep across the street, while a man passed us leading a group of others and swinging a crowbar. Back inside, I danced on the little stage; when a guy on Molly tried to hug me, Trevor gave him a double high five. And then, when we finally got back to his place and into bed, his ex-girlfriend called. Something she said made it clear -- she had been the threatening call before our date, her voice run through some kind of editing software, disguised. Now she was laughing at him, saying my date had probably gone badly. He said he was still on it. She got extremely pissed, told him never to call her again, and called back ten times. He didn't answer. He cried a little. I had a job interview at eleven the next morning, and instead I lay awake in the dark, his anxiety coming off him like heat, becoming mine -- a kind I hadn't felt in a while. It bothered me that he could be so obsessed with this other girl while we were lying in the same bed. I cuddled him at first. Then I stopped. In the morning he drove me to my interview and waited in the car, napping. We had a long kiss before I got out. We made rough plans to see each other again.

name: Gabriel
dek: A policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive.
pages:
We exchanged about six sentences on OkCupid before he asked if I wanted to hang out. The plan: overalls, Hot Topic, ironic. Then on the day of our date he announced he'd been "just kidding" about the overalls -- he'd rather do a park. I didn't like that. I told him to meet me at my house. He said I could be a murderer, or a rapist, and that he'd rather meet somewhere public. Not entirely unreasonable -- in another mood I might have admired the disregard for gender norms -- but I reconsidered whether I wanted to meet him at all, and cancelled our date right then and there. He seemed surprised. So I changed my mind.
I went into my room to make sure I was wearing clothes that didn't scream "I don't care if you think I'm pretty": a white ruffly button-down I'd never once considered wearing, which I thought perfect for my current sentiments. Roll-on deodorant. And, since I was going all out, I combed my hair with my fingers and got engrossed in how much I could change its state. Then, since I had to wait for his call, I fell backwards onto my bed and lay there half-dreaming about absolutely nothing -- and missed his call by seven minutes. He didn't pick up when I called back, so I texted him pictures of food and animals and smileys blowing heart kisses, walked the three houses to our meeting spot, and settled down next to a yield sign to study the percentage of white flowers embedded in the grass. I hadn't been outside yet that day; the gentle sun mushed my shoulders forward, sweetly. When he finally called, he was a few streets away, coming from work painting houses. His boss had criticized his work and cited it as the reason for his less-than-ideal pay, to which he'd replied: "then it's great that you're paying me what you are." I suggested this might have been a less than strategic response. Then I asked if we could meet for only a very short time, so we wouldn't have to suffer through an entire date -- and caught myself: this reluctance, this uneasiness, was exactly the quality I hated most in my own dates. So I left it at an invitation to my little intersection of white-flowered grass, and told him to see me not as a date but as a friend to be funny with. He came into view riding his bike like a steed -- sitting fully upright, since his hands were cradling the phone.

I told him I liked his pants, and that was the last I saw of him, as I have a policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive -- a policy that had come into effect, for the first time, that day. "Are you smoking a cigarette?" I asked. I wouldn't have to ask, he pointed out, if I'd been looking at him -- which was one hundred percent the case -- and I fell down laughing on the grass, imagining having to explain the policy's reasoning to him. His pants were spattered with paint from his job, and he was disappointed, he said, that people always commented on them; they were just his work clothes, so he didn't think they were cool. What I ideally would have noticed was the gold chain underneath the rim of his t-shirt. I noted that I did not have x-ray vision. This elaborate reasoning escaped him. I told him I would start looking at him, and that I was weird, and after convincing myself everything was the way it always was, I shifted my head in his direction for a second while he talked. I was very proud of myself.
His ex-girlfriend, he told me, had decided to become a stripper because she wanted her life to be more "real" -- he seemed to find this silly, so I was, of course, compelled to tell him that I was an "aspiring alcoholic" for a surprisingly similar reason. He said everyone in this park was on an OkCupid date, and pointed at a couple in front of us who weren't wearing much: that was the way to do it -- we should have come in our bathing suits. He was mostly looking to make friends in Portland, he said, since all his childhood friends had become gangster drug-addicts. I said I had no friends either, having only recently moved. We decided on beers from a store, and while he went inside he told me to watch his bike -- and then, that I should not walk off with it. I was surprised, and could think of no reason he would distrust me. I felt, suddenly, profoundly misunderstood. There was nothing I could do. He came back with a paper bag and we drifted to another park, first the ground, then a picnic table, where he told me he liked to dress up sometimes -- as a goth, in white tracksuits, as a gangster -- and I told him I didn't know many boys who liked to play dress-up. I told him what had happened with David, went to show him a picture, and found that I had been unmatched.

I chugged the last third of my beer and stood up feeling unhealthily drunk -- the air gone opaque, a darker, deeper blue -- and assigned myself the task of being extra careful about what came out of my mouth. He didn't want to pay for my dinner, he said; then, trying to explain himself, that he didn't want to pay for his own dinner either. At Los Gorditos I ordered a chimichanga much too large to finish, and we ate mostly in silence. After the meal he announced that he'd eaten too much and felt sick -- where others might have hidden this, he was straightforward, as though it should be my problem too. How could one ask for support so casually? I told him he could come sit on my couch for a moment to feel better.
At home, I pulled every piece of clothing out of my closet and introduced him to them one by one; his favorite was a bright orange long sleeve with a hologram of a dinosaur. He asked what I'd be doing if he weren't there, and I said, honestly, that I'd probably be on OkCupid -- so he made me go on it while he watched. I'd been messaging someone about reading poetry to each other; Gabriel said I should just write "let's have sex," so I did. The responses arrived over the next few hours -- first that he lived in North Portland and wanted foreplay, then "Oh I get it. Oh haha like 'we do sex now,'" then a third, something about poetry again. He saw my drawings and paintings and said, strangely: "Oh, I could actually use you for something -- I really need to learn how to paint and draw. You could teach me." It is and has been my dream to give art lessons to a willing pupil, so I feigned disinterest, then thought better of it and told him I was seriously interested.
When it got late, he said if he was going to bike home he'd better go. Outside, in the dark, standing behind his bike, he was just a glowy outline of a person -- white, not much height, but some sort of presence -- looking so forlorn. I'd stayed on the porch, under the light, leaving him no opportunity to hug or kiss me goodnight, which is perhaps what I intended. I said he could sleep on the couch if he really didn't want to bike; he said he would feel degraded to sleep on the couch. "Do you still want to do art lessons soon?" I asked, and he said, "Oh yeah -- can I just, like, start coming by if I'm in the neighborhood?" I asked if he was being sarcastic, since that seemed a strange thing to ask at the end of a first date. He biked off -- then called twenty-five minutes later: he'd forgotten his backpack. He came back for it, and this time I gave him a hug goodnight.

name: Michael
dek: I'd known him for months. His profile picture was blurry.
pages: Michael and I had known each other for months before I realized I was also talking to him on OkCupid. We'd matched. His profile picture was blurry, and I never connected the two people. In person we met at the Southeast Grind, on numerous occasions, none of which turned into hanging out anywhere else, or exchanging numbers, or making plans. The first time, he kept most of his eye contact on his phone, scrolling and clicking, glancing up at me every now and then while still, amazingly, managing to dominate the conversation, which was about which college major makes the most money. I stayed in it only because it was so ridiculous, and I was waiting for my chance to point out how rude he was being. Then he got interested enough to put the phone down, and I lost the urge to correct him, because the conversation was actually sort of interesting. After that we didn't greet each other as friends. More as patrons of the same establishment, passing the time. Though he did sit next to me, if we came in at once. One night he was already sitting with a boy named Matt, an activist, whom I liked a lot for his passion and soon found unreasonably idealistic, and the three of us went to the all-night pancake house, so it wasn't really a date. There we met a homeless man named Jason, and I invited him to our table too, without realizing how batshit he was. At some point he proposed. He asked me to marry him, and before I could answer he was pulling the pink glass ring off his own finger to give to me. It stuck. He kept pulling. By the time it came free his finger was bleeding, so now there was blood on the table, and a ring, and a proposal, and I asked for a bandaid because I felt guilty, like maybe I wasn't supposed to have been talking to him at all. By the end Michael and I were the only ones left, making jokes about Jason. His tactic for closing out a night, I learned, was agree-and-then-ignore: oh yeah, it's getting very late, we should probably go home, a laugh, and then a new topic, until I leaned back against the wall of the booth and fell asleep for a moment. Somewhere in there we invented niplr, a dating site where people meet based solely on pictures of each other's nipples. He also wanted an app where you pay for your food in line, which I thought was much too practical, and I wasn't sure he understood the game we were playing anymore. My therapist drove by the cafe, saw us in the window, knew exactly what he was looking at, and whisked me away. You should just date that guy, he said, once he had me. I think he felt guilty for taking me.

Then, on OkCupid, we kept up an inane conversation of nonsense until he invited me to a makerspace that happened to be two blocks from where I was standing. When I got there he was deep in conversation with a girl about which colleges they'd gone to. I joined by standing next to them, unacknowledged, until Michael waved a hand at me and said I'd also gone to college in Boston. I'd gone to college in Connecticut. Still, I was mildly impressed he'd remembered anything at all. He went off to make himself a name tag and came back as lobster bisque. I wasn't sure this was funny, but told myself perhaps I just didn't understand the joke. Mine said Sophie, and I told the girl that wasn't even my real name, that I'd been Sage, and she told me I was a coward for changing it to something more normal. That wasn't the reason I'd given, but I liked hers better, so I pretended to identify with it. I had two separate panic attacks about which beer to drink, poured one out behind the station, and was still undecided when Michael wandered over, hesitantly, and I bridged the gap between us. I told him a story I probably shouldn't have, about the night before. He said no, the story was very good, and that we should tell all the people at the party. We looked around. We didn't want to tell any of them. We decided to write a comic book. We founded niplr properly, he made a folder for it on his computer right there, while the girl he'd been talking to wandered the party alone, stopping near us sometimes to stare, and I kept saying we should include her and then going back on it, because I didn't actually want to. A boy's ping-pong ball rolled over to me. I picked it up and refused to give it back, so he had to come to me to retrieve it. When the party wrapped, Michael smuggled his beer cup out against his waist, and we walked to his apartment, a longer walk than I anticipated, possibly because I was by then quite drunk, having eaten almost nothing all day except a handful of sample macaroni and cheese I took from New Seasons with my hands on the way through, leaving by the back entrance. Somewhere in there I hurled my packet of memes into the dog cage I had once been in, myself. At his place I was too drunk for anything but the sofa, and then the porch, where a woman passing by, moving out of her apartment it looked like, gave me two packets of ramen, because I asked her for food. She and Michael had a conversation over my head. I don't know what it was about. I wasn't paying attention.

name: Jon
dek: Everything I didn't say.
pages:
The first OkCupid date I went on in Portland, I'd spent a whole week messaging men and meeting exactly none of them. Jon Storch broke the streak — mostly because I mentioned I was going to an art museum and he decided that counted as an invitation.
I dressed in about four minutes. I looked good, which annoyed me slightly, because I hadn't tried.
I met him fresh off raw fish and a Sapporo with my friend Alpha, who sized him up, gave him one minute of conversation, and left. Jon looked relieved. He took Alpha's seat, and when I offered him food and beer he wanted neither and went a little pale — I'm fairly sure he thought I was fattening him up for the check. Maroon hipster sweater. Tight jeans. Gaunt in the face, skinny everywhere else.
He talked. Brown, his administration, the newspaper he wrote for, the president who'd resigned in scandal. Here's the thing I never told him: I watched that woman resign. In person. At my brother's graduation. From Brown. I knew exactly who she was, and I sat there and let him explain her to me like a stranger. I nodded a lot. I faked opinions about liberalism I did not have. Then I paid the check with my debit card, which, for reasons I still can't defend, I found hilarious.

Then came the museum tour of a lifetime, if your life is very boring. The Korean prints did nothing for either of us. But I turned a corner and hit a clay sculpture — a little table of shiny, crowned white people — and something lit up. First thing all day. I leaned against the elevator wall and told myself everything was going to be okay. I don't know why I needed to hear it. Apparently I did.
Highlight of the date: a strange man at a suit of armor. It was tiny, built for the world's smallest, angriest warrior, and he just started talking to me, confident and funny, while Jon hovered a few feet back. And I ran a full internal debate: do I signal I'm on a date, or talk to this man more, so my actual date understands I'm not especially invested? Reader, I kept talking to the armor guy.
By the modern wing I came back to life, and by the time we left there was real camaraderie between us, mostly built on agreeing no one should put this much art in one building. But here's what I actually walked out thinking: it had been weirdly hard to say anything true to him all day. And I realized, right there on the steps, that I might be better off alone. At least alone I still get to have my own thoughts. He knew the books; I knew the art; neither of us had any idea what to do about it. But I'll give him this — he was smart. Smarter about school than I'll ever bother to be.

name: Pratfaller
dek: Thick pancakes in the morning, then he asked me to leave.
pages:
He let me sleep in his bed with him but I refused to let him kiss me
He made me thick pancakes in the morning
He asked me to leave so he could get ready for work
He was playing a rap song called "animal" that I liked
We tried riding home on his bike with me on his back
He offered to pay for a taxi for me
He said he was a very good car salesman and worked so much that he needed to use OkCupid
He switched my drink order to non-alcoholic
He paid for everything, including the drinks I'd had before he came
He shared a room with a girl he was not dating
As dictated by our weekly Vision Action Group Meetings, I had an all day meeting with my friend Joey. When the meeting seemed to be dragging I asked if it would make sense if I left him with some alone time. He didn’t mind my being there, he said, before locking himself in the bathroom for half an hour and coming out to tell me some alone time was what was called for. I left with the unnecessary awkwardness of the situation lingering in the pit of my stomach. Instead of going home I had a drink at a sushi restaurant on Alberta. After I’d been sitting at the bar by myself for about a half an hour I thought of a potential solution. I fired up the ol’ dating app and started inviting people to meet me. I invited three people and two responded and one came and his name I don’t remember.
I’d been sitting in the same swivel stool for an hour and a half by myself, wondering why my life was so boring and what the difference between being alive and dead really was in this moment when suddenly this lanky blonde man came in, nonchalantly taking a seat next to me. He ordered a drink and struck up a conversation as though we had no meeting planned.
After I'd been sitting at the bar myself I started asking people to meet me. I asked three people and two of them responded and one came and his name I don't remember (it was jake, I think) but his username was pratfaller. I'd been sitting there for an hour and a half by myself and suddenly this lanky tall blonde-haired guy came in, acting nonchalant as though he didn't know me and took a seat next to me at the bar and started talking to the bartender and ordering a drink. I suppose his plan was to tell people we just started chatting at this bar, and never mention the existence of our online communication.
But we got chatting and he told me he was a very good car salesman and that the only reason he was on okcupid is because he worked so often that he didn't have time to meet people. Strange I had never felt the need to excuse my online dating profile (my life’s blood, the precious gem of my existence). He worked sixty hours a week. He'd lived in Portland all his life he liked biking he made a lot of money he didn't like his job that much but he was good at it. I was a little gone; I’d already had two drinks and he bought me a third and himself a third too. I got up to go to the bathroom and remember the revelation of walking down the hall without the pressure of my meeting people costume and trying to have a realization about something about life and nothing was coming to me.
When we got up to leave, he paid for not just the drinks he'd ordered with me but the drinks I'd had before he came with his plastic money machine and signed a white little paper. He took me to a bar down the street and we sat at the counter on two black bar stools. He seemed to know the waitress there and talked to her for a minute while I went on my phone or something and then he ordered a different drink than I asked him to order: one without alcohol. It took me a little longer than it should have to figure out what he'd done and then I was disappointed because I wanted to get a little more intoxicated I was slipping off my bar stool and messing around with my purse backpack and left to go sit at the fire pit. I sat there and thought about being unhappy.
He came to sit next to me and I was feeling warm and sleepy and not like pretending anything anymore. I have no idea what we talked about; if anything I think he revealed that my new drink didn't have alcohol. He said his apartment was a 20 minute walk and that I could come if I wanted to. So I suppose I said yes because next thing I knew we were out in the cold night again, traveling for what seemed like forever to a place I’d never been before that I could not imagine actually existing
I wasn't wearing pants; instead I was wearing a skirt. I kept asking him how much longer the walk was going to be and he kept saying like 20 minutes. He had his bike and he said he'd have a cab called for me if I wanted and that we could see each other again but I was stubborn and we continued the journey. He offered to have me ride on his back as he biked. It was extremely hard to get on and I wobbled off almost as soon a we started moving. He said we should try again but it wasn't a good experience and he wasn't being nice to me so I said no we could just walk the rest of the way. It took a lot longer. I was drunk and said whatever came into my head. I wasn't walking very straight either; I remember my limbs were falling all over each other sort of and I felt sort of like a frat bro. I felt like a very clumsy girl. I couldn’t tell if he liked me at all. I didn’t like him too much then either, since he kept saying slightly mean things to me about my being drunk my not having a job.
His building was unexpectedly tall, sleek, and shiny. There was even a lobby with brown carpet and marbled tiles. And to my surprise, we weren’t even the only one’s arriving here this late; in fact about 5 other people took the elevator alongside us.
I was excited to be inside. I didn't look at him and he didn't look at me. It was a really silent and calm experience after that strange walk and I felt nothing like I’d felt outside in this warm refuge. When we got into his little apartment I was surprised to find that he had a female roommate, who’d apparently agreed to sleep on the couch due to my presence. She was small, and maybe Asian, and had all her bed things settled there; a brown duvet, and a fluffy white pillow. I talked to her for a bit before dropping all my things onto the floor in his bedroom where we slept on his twin, perhaps cuddling but I refused to let him kiss me. I don’t know why. I simply didn’t want it to happen.
In the morning he was already awake, tossing some pancakes which we ate at his high table. I remember he had a little speaker over which he played an upbeat rap song which I liked, and I asked him for the artist. I do not know what the mood was that morning; I was very grateful to him for making me pancakes, especially after not letting him kiss me. I don’t think either of us knew if we’d ever see each other again as we boarded the elevator so that he could be on his way to work.

name: Sean
dek: The least successful Tinder date of all.
pages:
This was perhaps the least successful tinder date of all and actually ended in something like a fight.
After spending the night at Jake’s house, I was relatively stranded in a part of town that I did not recognize. I figured this was as a good a time as any to get to know new parts of the city, and found myself in a sports bar with a balcony overlooking giant tvs. Instead of a bar, they had picnic tables dispersed scattered throughout and I spent most of the day here. I talked to a friend on the phone as I wandered upstairs though that part was roped off and thought dejectedly about my constant, nagging loneliness. How could it be this hard to find people to shoot the shit with, besides my friend’s back home?
I left and made plans to meet Sean Niesson on the corner of Everett and 18th….it was kind of a strange place to wait, and I felt rather self-conscious as cars whizzed past me, probably wondering what I was doing standing in the middle of nowhere.
It was then, of course, after I’d finally secured plans, that my roommate Alpha asked if I wanted to meet him at The Economics of Happiness Conference which was downtown. I said I would meet him and go out for dinner with him and a group of friends he'd met at the conference. Sean picked me up on the street corner of Everett and 19th. I remember because I waited in that corner for quite a while, unsure if I'd be waiting there forever. I got into the car and he was immediately unfriendly. I don't remember what we talked about.
When I got in the car, he did not smile, and barely looked up. Rather than friendly banter, his hands were glued to the steering wheel, his eyes fixed on the road. I have to say I pride myself on being somewhat of an expert at drawing even the stubbornest introvert into casual conversation, but this time it was really like pulling teeth.
The only thing I remember from this conversation is him being surprised that I had a friend, one friend, who lived in Portland, having lived there for three months. He told me he still hung out with his friend from high school, which didn’t sound too bad to be honest.
The conference took place in a large hall, that felt a bit like a church I’d been to once. The seating was stadium style, and the seats were beige, and cushioned. I can understand, in retrospect, that I might not have been the ideal date, at least from his perspective. While he paid rapt attention to the goings on below, I surreptitiously looked at my phone, which had me quite addicted at this point in my life.
It was the last day of a three day conference, and there was a ceremony wherein everyone was invited to get up and dance. At this point, we switched roles to some extent as he faded shyly into the background, and I joined the lively procession from the hall to the lobby.
Outside, we settled on a nearby bar, the cheerful tortoise which I’d never been to before, and as we walked the five blocks over the cobbled stones of downtown Portland, I was somewhat surprised to hear that he’d taken in the message, not to mention on board with its way of seeing the world. Though I hadn’t, perhaps, been paying full attention, I’d managed to take in enough to know I had my doubts, and tried, a bit unsuccessfully, to explain my skepticism. Oh, what was I doing anyway, casting aspersions on what seemed to be an inspiring experience for the young lad?
At the bar, I asked for a dinner menu. This is when our date, which hadn’t been going particularly well up until this point, sort of imploded. It would seem that he was under the impression that I was trying to get him to buy me dinner. Having had nothing but those thick pancakes early that morning, and having finally arrived at an establishment meant for eating, my mind was occupied with nothing but my sudden realization of hunger. He paid for our beers, and we left, but as we walked back into the street, we sort of stopped interacting, and he left without so much as a “bye.”
I was now out on the streets of Portland by myself and it was getting dark. What’s more, my phone wasn’t charged. However, I managed to find an outlet hidden at the base of a telephone pole and just in the nick of time too, as I’d forgotten I’d apparently scheduled another date that was supposed to starting imminently. In fact, unbeknownst to me, a man had driven from nearby Beaverton, and was sitting, now, in his car, waiting to meet me.

name: Matt
dek: One tiny blurry picture of him playing a red guitar.
pages:
Matt’s had only one picture on his profile and it was tiny and blurry and depicted him playing a red guitar. However, our conversation on okcupid had entered the realm of absurdity and I was excited to meet someone who’d been conversing with me exclusively about chickens for a day or two.
He appeared above my perch by the telephone pole, where I was huddled, still trying to charge my phone. He wasn’t quite as skinny as those few pixels had made him seem, and he was wearing a gray sweatshirt. He told me his plan was to go to Ground Kontrol, a bar that doubles as an arcade. But at this point, I was all but starving so I redirected us to the nearest restaurant which was a sophisticated Italian place with counter service and only about 5 dishes on the menu. We split a plate of pasta and a beer and, after my previous date, we split the tab as well.
Afterwards we did go to Ground Kontrol. When I asked him if he’d had much luck on okcupid, he told me a story about the other girl he'd met on okcupid who he didn't like. Apparently she texted him that she had been waiting in her car for a while and had gotten very sweaty. I started talking to this guy at the booth next to us who was from Colorado. Then my date and I left. He offered to drive me home. I was a little bit drunk and I discovered I'd forgotten to close my tab so he drove me back to Ground Kontrol and I recovered my debit card. In the car outside my house he gave me a tiny kiss on the lips before I got out. I went inside and saw that he had texted me that he was sorry if he'd "forced the kiss on me." I didn’t respond
I felt awkward as he hadn’t particularly forced me to kiss him, though I can’t say I wanted it to happen either. Unsure of how to respond, I didn’t. And later, I found out he’d deleted his okcupid after that, apparently so embarrassed about this ambiguous interaction that he’d wanted his online presence to disappear.
A few months later, I sent him the invitation for writing a synopsis of how our date went. He didn't write one but called me one night while I was having dinner with my roommates. I took the call in the bathroom. He told me that he hadn't been on any other okcupid dates after ours and that he thought okcupid was home to the kind of girls he didn't like. It seemed like he meant basic bitches. He said that he'd been confused because he'd thought our date had gone really well but after it was over he reconsidered why he thought that and couldn't come up with any reasons. He said that I'd seemed very nervous throughout the date and thought I must have been nervous to be on a date with him but considered that I might somehow be fucking with him and just pretending to be nervous. He said he didn't know why he'd had us go to Ground Kontrol and that it was because he had planned it and so it was set in his mind. I was enjoying our conversation and laughing a lot. He told me a story about his roommate peeing on his living room rug that I found hard to believe. I told him I might hang out with him as friends in a few weeks after I became not so busy.

name: Kyle
dek: In one picture, a chin like a witch.
pages:
In most of his pictures he looked normal - skinny, with pale skin, my type. In one picture, it appeared he had a pointed chin, like a witch. I wondered - was this the most accurate representation of what he actually looked like in real life? I messaged him for a while, I asked him first for a drum lesson and he countered with: coffee or tea? he asked if I thought that was too forward and he interpreted my "yes" as "yes that was too forward."
I exchanged a phone number with him, but still had surprising difficulty agreeing on a where and when to meet, even after conversing verbally multiple times. Finally, I led him to my favorite spot, due mostly to convenience (the Southeast Grind) for a coffee or tea or something, though it was already really late at night.
I got there before him, I ordered a chai tea that I did not want but felt obligated to consume anyways, I got a call from him, he arrived on his bicycle; I did not see him when I went outside to look and became concerned that I'd given him directions to the wrong place.
Then I saw him, he had the thing I'd thought his face might look like in his profile, sort of like a witches, with a pointy chin and I thought he was also attractive, more so than my last date at least. He was wearing a sleek black "biking' jacket and I think shorts, which I suppose did not become him (his personality). We hugged.
He didn't order anything in the cafe, he wanted to go to subway, there was some awkward confusion with me trying to make up a reason why I would also want to go to Subway but it turned out he didn’t care one way or the other. He seemed not incredibly mindful of what I might be thinking at any given moment. We went to subway. In the line, we talked about our parents, and their jobs.
After we walked the few blocks to his drum studio (about 10), and we made forced and very awkward conversation in the small carpeted space that he was renting.
I was beginning to feel rather nonplussed by this experience when he showed me what he could do with drumsticks. In spite of myself, I was impressed, though less so that he seemed to know and think it was impressive himself, too. We sat across from each other at the makeshift table in amidst various stands and paraphernalia, awkwardly perusing each other’s music libraries, noting intermittently when we recognized or liked a song in common.
It wasn’t going very well; and for a moment I felt I’d been transported back to middle school - unable to carry on a full conversation with the opposite gender, reduced to blushes and quick glances of eye contact. I don’t think I knew what he was thinking. I felt for sure he could have ended the date at any time had he not been into me so I assumed shyness. We plodded on, and finally we had had enough and agreed it was time to go. But first I asked to use the bathroom and he showed me the way. He noted offhandedly that it was cold and I offered him my coat. Veering from his script, he suggested that we switch outfits altogether, and so we did. He tried on the black evening gown I’d purchased for \$6.99 from Goodwill earlier that day, and I put on whatever he was wearing.
There was something incredibly comical about the large protrusion that appeared suddenly in the front, lower half of the dress, bunching the silken material, rippling outward. Back in the little room he was renting, I picked up one of the wooden sticks that littered the floor and used it to find the indentation of his belly button, then penetrated it rhythmically.
After we spent a bit more time in the studio, he walked me home and slept in my bed. In the morning he told me really liked me, and went off to school.
alternate: Memoir - 3 days ago - with Kyle
Kyle went with me to the subway where he got a foot long with all the veggies but olives and extra jalapenos. I got a 6 inch with pepper jack and vegetables and olives and mustard on it whereas he brought chipotle sauce and we sat at a table and he had his whereas I put mine away in my backpack. In the line he told me he knew computer programming because he liked web design. I told him I had moved to Portland from Connecticut and California before whereas he had moved to Portland to go to PSU and his parents kept changing where they liked for his father’s job which was for pharmaceuticals - he didn’t know what disease his dad was caring but I said it was probably Parkinson’s which was a disease I learned about in neuroscience. We went to the practice room where he plays his instrument because he wanted to show me. It took a while to set it up which he was embarrassed and kept telling me he was sorry for it taking so long for him to put all the different parts onto the drumset with screws. When he was done he played a long drum solo which was pretty crazy and I liked it. His body was very active during the solo which made me imagine him doing stuff in bed like slapping or kicking or punching or pinching me which he did later after i played a little. When I went inside I saw a red-haired boy sitting at a table by himself. He had a laptop and a brief case and a mess of papers set out in front of him. He had a green teapot on the table. I always wondered who drank tea at this place when it was about \$6 for a cup and all it included was hot water and a tea bag.
I left my groceries outside as I could see them from the window, and slumped down onto the couch, every now and then staring at the boy with the red hair without either of us saying anything. His head was behind the tea pot but I could still see his eyes. It seemed he was intermittently stopping what he was doing just to stare at me.
Eventually I got up to go home but came back in to put the cup and spoon away I'd used to eat my cereal. It was then that he approached me and said he had to at least talk to the person he'd been staring at for the past hour or so. Yes! Success. He helped me carry my groceries back to my house and hung around in my room a little while I put them away. He told me he was on his way to two parties and though I'd decided somewhere around that time that he wasn't quite as interesting as his blue eyes had at first suggested, I agreed to accompany him on his evening out, interested in a change of scenery.
We walked back to the grind together where it was revealed that unlike me who got everywhere on foot, he actually had a car. It wasn't a great car - it was old and kind of small and probably a whitish brown color. The backseat, like his table, was piled high with paperwork. On the way we chatted about this and that - what I did for a living and what he did.
The first party was at a beautiful house where everyone was quite friendly. Everyone assumed I was his girlfriend and we had a strange time explaining that we'd met just an hour earlier at a coffee shop.
Ryan went off to sit on the counter in the kitchen and drink beer with his friend who he had not seen in a long time and I joined the rest of the party where they were in the middle of explaining a strange game which involved many different-colored plastic pyramids which could be stacked on top of each other to win the game. Although it looked fun, the rules were inexcusably complex and the objective seemed like an afterthought.
More and more people were joining our table and needed the rules to be explained again and again. It emerged that one small gray triangle was missing, and that we had gotten most of the rules wrong. Claire, thin and waifish who was steering the game had a special smile as if to say "we would never play monopoly." and her partner Brandon, seemed used to following her lead, and only a bit like there was something wrong with his brain that his attractiveness was making up for. He had a crew cut to match his sad blue eyes.
Claire and I were similarly enthusiastic about anything and everything - whether it made sense to be or not. Ryan and I had to go - there was another party his main best friend's birthday at a restaurant in downtown - but not before I mentioned to Claire that I was looking for a job and Claire told me to apply at a summer camp for especially intelligent children who wanted to use their summer to sew and to program computers. I jotted down my contact details and we left to drive 15 miles across town; all the while he was explaining his weed business to me. I think I somehow managed to give him the impression that I was both impressed and interested so that's what we talked about when we stopped at lights. It was very dark and there were lots of winding roads. I couldn't be sure I'd ever been to this part of Portland even during the day.
After he had built up the party so much, saying how it was his very best friend so he couldn't miss it, no one was really paying any attention to us. we were sitting on the end away from his friend.
We were playing Never Have I Ever which someone had apparently taken the time to make into an actual board game version with cards and stuff. Except no one seemed to have done anything that the cards said and everyone had these nervous smiles like they were trying not to let anyone into their thoughts.
We agreed that we were both hungry and decided to leave and get crepes. We walked to a crepe place and talked about the part of town we were in. We ordered a banana Nutella crepe to share and discussed what it meant to date and variations to the norm concept like dating multiple people or dating people of the same gender. He addressed the topic as though I might not have considered it before, strangely, and seemed to be informing me of alternatives to a way of thinking I had not expressed explicitly. I suppose he lumped me in with mainstream opinions. It reminded me a little of how my first boyfriend liked to tell me about things he knew and thought I didn't.
When the check came (about \$7.50 for the crepe we’d shared), he eyed me mischievously, and asked me conspiratorially if I wanted to put what I had just learned from him to the test. So we split the check.
Then we drove to his house, which seemed a bit on the outskirts of town. Instead of a mattress, he simply had lots of pillows and blankets bunched together on the floor (he said he’d just moved in). My eyes glanced around his room; there was a bookshelf with many unknown treasures. The floor was pleasant hardwood, and seemed clean (he had just moved in).
Then we went into the kitchen and he stood in front of the cabinet while I sat on the counter while we talked about the different kinds of tea he had and I told him I didn't really like tea. He got two mugs and boiled water and put the bags in those little metal steeping ball things. I think I picked chamomile.
We laid on the couch together for a while with his head on my lap (he asked if it was ok to put it there) and then went into his room and he told me I could pick out a big shirt from his closet to wear to bed and made a point of closing his eyes while I changed in the space between his closet and his "bed" which was just a pile of blankets on the floor. His room was sparse and it had lots of CDs and small things on the wall. He had a bit of weed paraphernalia on it too, and a tan bookshelf with a lot of books in it. We told each other stories as we were falling asleep and in the morning he woke up early and left the room and then he came back so we could cuddle.
In the morning, he asked if I wanted to come grocery shopping with him and he drove us even farther out of town, to a Korean Grocery Store he apparently frequented, and he bought things that I’d never heard of - various kinds of noodles, and seaweed, and I looked for those jelly cup things my mom used to buy my brother and I, hoping to reminisce about how we’d smush them out into our mouths as young children.
Then he drove me back to the place we’d started - my little blue house where my two roommates were chatting amiably on the couch. Though we’d now spent almost 24 hours together, I invited him inside.
He said he hadn't considered coming inside but that now he was here he might as well. My roommates were both there when we got in and I sat at the chair at the table while he sat on the couch and my roommate lay at the other end. We told them what we had done on our date. It turned out he had helped my roommate book a show a long time ago.
He returned a minute after he left because he'd forgotten to get my number and kissed me (for the first time) on the lips behind the curtain that closed off the kitchen so my roommates didn't see.
After he left, both of my roommates told me that they liked him and that I should invest in him. They said he was attractive. Alpha said that we seemed to have some chemistry. Later that week, Greg told me I should stop going on dates with other people and just try to go out with him again.
I didn't have my phone so I couldn't text him until Thursday when I went to retrieve it from David's house and then I texted him excitedly except he only replied in one word answers so I gave up. I called him when I decided to take the job I'd been offered at the party he took me to and he called me back about a week later but didn't return my call after that. I ran into him a long time after that when I was walking towards a library with Westley and he walked in the opposite direction as soon as I saw him but when I made eye contact and casually said hi to him he said hi back.

name: Kyle II

pages:
(from kyle's perspective):
I think you'll appreciate the irony of the situation.
So I took someone's advice and have been trying internet dating and it is something.
I can't quite rank up the strangeness of the dates I've been on but this might be #1 out of a small number, yet. But I already know I'm a strange attractor.
I'm unsure of the ratio on the site but the men vastly outnumber the ladies, I'm fairly certain. So it came to my surprise when a woman messaged me saying I looked interesting but how could she be certain? So I assured her I was who I am and exchanged some messages - soon enough I asked her if she would go out for coffee with me and she replied yes: either sometime later in the year or at 4 AM next week.
Pfft. All I could think was why not? I wasn't all that worried about having my organs harvested and where do you get coffee at 4 AM anyway? So I asked where and there is a place, yay verily, there is a place. So fast forwards to the day or late night we finally set upon and eventually the texts start volleying around 1 AM when I learn she's at a bar and needs a ride. So with a hop-skip and a-do I arrive to meet her.
She's at least sober which was different than another person/place but she told me she had been up for over 24 hours, which as I was already asking -- tweaker? Poker face already engaged we had a nice chat at the bar for awhile, her asking about my life, what I do, how's my luck with dating online, pleasant stuff and we shared a few things in common.
She did seem quite out of it, bobbing her head to the music, scribbling on a napkin, asking pretty personal questions, but fine, I just wanted to get to know someone, and that's what I was doing. I didn't want to drink all night and neither did she so we decided to go to the 24 hour coffee place she likes. That's where things get strange.
Soon as we mosey up to order coffee one of her old daters was already there to greet us. A regular 2 AM coffee addict no doubt. She told me he was a past date and they talk before ordering and me and him just exchange funny glances. A couple more awkward moments later I have my cup of java and we go to sit down. The past dater joins us for a bit but he got tired of standing and listening to my tired mind babbling for my date. A victory I'd take but it wouldn't last. My babbling continues and I at least have her laughing - at me or with me it didn't matter. Either way I had an attractive audience and things don't matter at 2 in the morning after being up all day prior.
She's a master of Socratic dialogue. She would pretend to know less than she let on and smirk at my mansplaining. She would ask questions of some of the stupid things I said and trip me up. But she made it clear she liked me. She asked if I knew where to get cocaine. "No" was my hasty reply. "No". I told her I tried it but not how dumb I consider it. All of a sudden look. Here's a guy walking in she went on two dates with. O.O. Poker face. Emptiness of thought and mind. I've prepared for stupid stuff like this dammit. Sometime later in our conversation I told her how nice it is to suffer from depersonalization at times.
She gets a call. A guy she dated last week wants to meet her and he's already on his way. Fine I tell her. Fine I don't care. She tells me she wants to get six of the smartest men she meets online and take them on a bus out into the wilderness where they will learn how to be better people. What's this called I ask? "Imagination Land" she tells me. Is there a walled compound involved? No, there's a castle. I think I must have slipped into that special 3 AM place which madmen witness on occasion. I felt alarmingly at home there.
Her other date cruises up on his long board and we go outside to meet him and his nice dog Hero. Hero was probably the greatest thing of that night. I've always liked dogs. Anyway we shake hands and make introductions. I share his joint and fight rising nausea. He tells me he's on acid, works at a marijuana dispensary, and studies English in college and then starts singing in German. I am an outside observer to the situation I find myself in I tell myself.
And to make this long story shorter we four including Hero went back to her place and hung out on her bed where she invited us to live with her for the next two days and dress us up in her cloths. I hugged and said my goodbyes not too long after. Haven't seen her since.

Finally this woman came to my table and I started asking about her shoes.
She was the kind of person who is happy to do all the talking and she started regaling me, and then this older guy with scratchy-looking hair and a baseball cap with stories that often seemed to lack a moral or clear catalyst for telling them.

As it was happening, I settled for philosophizing about the dynamics of why this happens in different situations and hoping that if I paid less and less attention to him that it would change. Instead I found myself making an extra effort to be interesting and witty.

name: Xander
